Definition: Percentage of the national population covered by at least one 4G/LTE mobile network signal, whether or not they subscribe to the service. 4G is the practical minimum for meaningful broadband connectivity enabling digital services.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Original source is a blog citing Djibouti Telecom's own August 2021 claim of 75% 4G coverage, not independently verified. GSMA's State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2022 explicitly lists Djibouti among the countries with the highest mobile broadband coverage gap worldwide, and a 2019 World Bank report found coverage 'far lower' than the regional average and concentrated in Djibouti City, both of which conflict with a 75-89% population coverage claim. Evidence is contradictory and no reliable independent percentage was found; marked Unknown pending human review to reconcile operator self-reporting with GSMA's coverage-gap assessment.

Definition: Percentage of individuals who used the internet (from any location, via any device) in the last three months. This measures actual internet adoption beyond network availability, capturing the combined effect of infrastructure, affordability, digital literacy, and relevance.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. DataReportal's Digital 2026 Djibouti report (65% individuals using the internet) is corroborated by an independent ITU-sourced figure of 65.30% for 2024 reported via TheGlobalEconomy.com. Both fall within the 50-69% band; Value Code 4 stands.

Definition: The country's total international internet bandwidth capacity per internet user, indicating the quality and capacity of the country's connection to the global internet. Determined by submarine cable landings (for coastal states), cross-border terrestrial fibre (for landlocked states), and satellite links.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The cited ITU country profile itself reports 76.6 kbit/s per internet user (2016), which falls in the 'Good (50-99 kbit/s)' band (Value Code 4), not 'Strong (100+)' (Value Code 5) as recorded — a scoring error against the source's own figure. No fresher country-specific ITU DataHub figure could be located during this review; the underlying data point is nearly a decade old and should be updated when newer ITU statistics become available.

Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and re-sourced from the weak original citation. AMS-IX Djibouti (DjIX) is active with roughly 20 connected networks including major international carriers and content networks (Cloudflare, China Telecom, China Mobile, MTN, Hurricane Electric, Liquid Telecom, Djibouti Telecom, Djibouti Data Center), indicating moderate, largely international-carrier participation rather than a broad domestic ISP ecosystem. Value Code 4 is a reasonable fit and is retained.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original figure (51.9%) is DataReportal/GSMA 'cellular mobile connections' as a share of population, not unique subscriber penetration as the variable explicitly requires (connections can exceed population due to multi-SIM ownership). A 2019 World Bank report citing 2018 GSMA data put Djibouti's unique subscriber penetration below 30%, lagging the Sub-Saharan Africa average of 45%. No fresher unique-subscriber-specific figure for Djibouti was found. Given the metric mismatch and absence of a current authoritative unique-subscriber statistic, marked Unknown pending human review rather than guessing a code from connections data.

Value Name: Regional cloud availability zone nearby (same sub-region)
Comments: Regional zones nearby (AWS UAE, Azure Qatar, Google SA); no local hyperscale
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: No local or near-local hyperscale cloud region was identified for Djibouti; nearest availability zones remain in the UAE, Qatar and South Africa, consistent with the original assessment. However, the cited source is a generic Middle East cloud-expansion article, not Djibouti-specific, and no better direct source was found. Value Code 3 is plausible and retained, but sourcing remains weak — flagged for human review if a more specific source becomes available.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
Comments: Proposed/planned in digital strategy, no comprehensive law yet
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original 'proposed/draft' assessment is outdated: Djibouti's Digital Code (Loi n°019/AN/23) was formally enacted on 30 June 2025, not merely proposed. It imposes cross-border data transfer restrictions requiring 'adequate protection' in the recipient jurisdiction — a sectoral/partial localisation-adjacent requirement — though it does not appear to mandate blanket in-country storage of all personal or government data. Revised to Value Code 3 (sectoral requirements only) on this basis; recommend human review to confirm whether implementing regulations impose stricter data-residency mandates.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted comprehensive data protection and privacy legislation. A foundational legal requirement for building trust in digital public infrastructure and for enabling secure cross-border data flows under frameworks like the AU Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection.
Value Name: Legislation enacted with Data Protection Authority established
Comments: Enacted in Digital Code June 2025 with CNDP DPA established
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The Digital Code (enacted 30 June 2025) does establish a comprehensive, GDPR-style data protection regime and designates the CNDP as supervisory authority, but both techhiveadvisory.africa and consentstack.io (reviewed November 2025) explicitly note the CNDP 'has not yet been operationally established.' Since the authority exists in law but is not yet functioning, this better fits Value Code 3 ('legislation enacted but no enforcement authority') than Value Code 4. Revised accordingly; should be re-raised to 4 once the CNDP is confirmed operational.

Comments: Wingu TO7 carrier-neutral data center launched, Djibouti Data Center exists; small-scale
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Fresher reporting (November 2024) confirms Wingu Africa's new T07 Technology Park facility is a certified Tier III data centre (3MW capacity), alongside the earlier Djibouti Data Center (2013). This meets the criterion for Value Code 3 ('at least one Tier III facility'), an upgrade from the 'small-scale Tier I-II only' assessment in Comments, which appears to have understated the new facility's certification.

Comments: Digital transformation strategy includes cloud services, data centers in national systems; basic operational
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with caveats. The Digital Economy Navigator country profile suggests a shared government cloud platform is 'in use', while a 2025 academic study on Djibouti's e-Cabinet describes the country as a 'low e-government maturity' context still building basic digital signature/e-identity infrastructure. These signals are mixed but consistent with a basic, still-developing government data centre/cloud capability. Value Code 3 retained; flagged for human review given conflicting maturity signals.

Definition: Whether the country has established policies, regulations, and programmes supporting off-grid and distributed energy solutions (mini-grids, solar home systems). These are critical for extending ICT infrastructure to unserved areas beyond the central grid.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and refreshed. A GEF/UNDP off-grid mini-grid programme has been under implementation through 2024, the Africa Minigrids Programme operates active sites (e.g. Yoboki village), and UNDP/government hosted a national rural-electrification-by-minigrid dialogue in July 2024. This shows continued active policy and deployment (Value Code 3), superseding the 2017 source; the original code is retained but re-evidenced with current material.

Definition: Frequency and severity of power outages experienced by businesses and households. Based on World Bank Enterprise Surveys, Afrobarometer, or national utility data. Reflects the quality of electricity supply beyond mere access — critical for running ICT equipment and data infrastructure.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The World Bank Enterprise Survey itself reports 'just under 2' outages per month (roughly 19-24 per year), which exceeds the '<10 per year' threshold for Value Code 4 ('Good') and instead fits Value Code 3 ('Moderate, monthly outages, occasional disruptions') — the original row miscoded its own cited figure. This data is also from 2013 and now over a decade old; a new Djibouti World Bank Enterprise Survey was fielded in late 2025 (microdata.worldbank.org/catalog/8253) but detailed infrastructure/outage results were not yet published at time of review — recommend re-checking once released.

Definition: Percentage of total electricity generation from renewable sources (hydro, solar, wind, geothermal, biomass). Indicates energy sustainability and potential for distributed power solutions relevant to ICT infrastructure in off-grid areas.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: The original Value Code (2, 10-24%) does not match its own comment (80%) — a clear internal inconsistency. Independent IRENA/EIA-based generation statistics (countryeconomy.com, corroborated by statbase.org and measuredworld.com) put Djibouti's renewable share of domestic electricity generation at approximately 35% in 2024 (Value Code 3, 25-49%), which is used here as the primary, methodologically standard figure. The Minister of Energy's ~80% claim (cited in the original source) and Djibouti Electricity's own 2024 figures appear to include imported Ethiopian hydroelectric power as part of the renewable supply mix rather than domestic 'generation' as strictly defined by this variable; this produces a materially different, higher figure. Flagged for human review to confirm which convention (generation vs. total supply including imports) the index intends.

Definition: The scale and quality of tertiary-level ICT and STEM education programmes available in the country, based on the number and quality of institutions offering ICT degrees, computer science programmes, and engineering courses relative to the population.
Comments: University of Djibouti has Faculty of Technology, Industrial Technology, Engineering; limited institutions
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed with better sourcing (the original citation was a low-quality directory site). The University of Djibouti remains effectively the country's sole comprehensive tertiary institution, though it houses a Faculty of Engineering (ICT, civil, electrical specialisms), a Faculty of Sciences with computer science, an Industrial Technology Institute, and hosts the Africa Centre of Excellence for Logistics and Transport (CEALT), which added a Master's in Data Science and doctoral engineering programmes from 2019. This is consistent with 'few institutions, low enrolment' — Value Code 2 retained.
